en: Yaka (Heinemann, 1996, tr. Marga Holness)
bl: Epic spanning a century of Angolan history through the Semedo family. Regarded as Pepetela's masterwork.

Four episodes following Angolan students in Lisbon, guerrilla fighters, and disillusioned post-independence intellectuals — a searing meditation on revolutionary idealism and its collapse. No confirmed English translation.
Buildings collapse around the lagoon of the mermaid spirit Kianda — allegory of post-independence disillusionment.

en: Ngunga's Adventures (Tanzania Publishing House, 1980)
bl: Written during the liberation war as an MPLA training text. A foundational text of Angolan national literature.
Comic detective novel parodying James Bond — satirises corruption and chaos in post-war Luanda.

t: Jaime Bunda e a Morte do Americano
bl: Second Jaime Bunda detective novel; sardonic adventures in a Luanda riven by oil money and intrigue.
An aging Angolan professor in California receives a message that disrupts his comfortable exile.
A shy man navigates romantic failure and middle-class Luandan life with characteristic Pepetela irony.
A state attorney investigates corruption among the Luandan elite — portrait of Angola's post-war predator class.
An ancestral mask becomes a symbol of authentic Angolan identity in the face of colonial cultural erasure.
Fantastical fable in an imaginary African village exploring community, environment and myth.

en: Luuanda (Heinemann, 1980, tr. Tamara L. Bender)
bl: Three stories set in Luanda's musseques, written in prison in a fusion of Kimbundu and Portuguese. The award caused PIDE to dissolve the Portuguese Writers Society.

t: A Vida Verdadeira de Domingos Xavier
en: The Real Life of Domingos Xavier (Heinemann, 1978, tr. Michael Wolfers)
bl: A tractor driver tortured to death for refusing to name comrades. Adapted as the landmark film Sambizanga (1972) by Sarah Maldoror.
Stream-of-consciousness memories of four childhood friends from Luanda driven by colonialism onto irreconcilable paths — war, resistance, survival.

en: A General Theory of Oblivion (Harvill Secker, 2015, tr. Daniel Hahn)
bl: A Portuguese woman bricks herself into her Luanda apartment as civil war rages outside for nearly thirty years.

en: The Book of Chameleons (Simon & Schuster, 2008, tr. Daniel Hahn)
bl: A gecko narrates the story of an albino man who invents genealogies for Angola's newly rich.
A TV producer arrives in Angola and encounters a country in the grip of petro-capitalism and historical amnesia.
Stories traversing Angola, Brazil and Portugal, linked by displacement and migration.
A woman travels across Africa collecting miraculous stories — celebrates oral tradition and interconnected lives.

en: My Father's Wives (Simon & Schuster, 2014, tr. Daniel Hahn)
bl: A young woman journeys across Africa seeking the women her father loved — road novel about identity and family secrets.
Early short fiction blending the magical and the political, rooted in Angolan and Brazilian landscapes.
Exploration of faith, doubt and the divine across multiple Lusophone continents and voices.
Stories centred on music and rhythm as organising metaphors for Angolan and Lusophone life.

en: Whites Can Dance Too (Faber & Faber, tr. Daniel Hahn)
bl: An Angolan musician detained at the Norwegian border; three narrators celebrate diaspora identity and kuduro. Co-founder of Buraka Som Sistema.

en: Good Morning Comrades (Biblioasis, 2008, tr. Stephen Henighan)
bl: Semi-autobiographical vignettes of childhood in 1980s Luanda — neighbourhood games, school, first love.
Lyrical coming-of-age novel navigating chaotic late-civil-war Luanda.
Lyrical novel centred on an old man who communicates through whistling — allegory of memory and language loss.
Ondjaki's debut: brief, fragmentary stories of Angolan life marked by tenderness and formal experimentation.
Beloved children's book about a magical bicycle with a moustache — celebrated across the Lusophone world.
Lyrical Angolan novel exploring land, belonging and the wounds of colonial dispossession.
Experimental Angolan novel questioning the boundaries between testimony, fiction and history.
Novel drawing on Angolan landscape and transformations of individual and collective identity.

t: A Última Lua de Homem Grande
bl: Angolan novel tracing the twilight years of a colonial-era patriarch and the memories that surface.
An 'affectionate dictionary' by four Lusophone writers from Angola, Portugal and Brazil — alphabetically ordered entries on universal themes.

t: Com a Saliva Muito ao Sul
bl: Angolan poetry collection traversing memory and southern landscape.
Collaborative Lusophone collection exploring Blackness, beauty and identity.
Text by Angolan politician and CASA-CE opposition leader — exact title unclear from spine.

en: Sleepwalking Land (Serpent's Tail, 2006, tr. David Brookshaw)
aw: One of 12 Best African Books of the 20th Century (Zimbabwe Book Fair)
bl: An old man and a boy travel through war-devastated Mozambique, finding comfort in a young man's hidden diaries.

en: The Tuner of Silences (Biblioasis, 2013, tr. David Brookshaw)
bl: A family shelters indoors while a petrified rain falls outside — magical novella meditating on memory and silence.
A young doctor investigates a general's death in colonial Mozambique — slow, atmospheric novel interrogating colonial power. No confirmed English translation.

en: Woman of the Ashes (FSG, 2018, tr. David Brookshaw)
bl: First of the Sands of the Emperor trilogy: a Mozambican woman and Portuguese soldier narrate as colonial conquest unfolds.

en: The Drinker of Horizons (FSG, 2020, tr. David Brookshaw)
bl: Third and final volume of the Sands of the Emperor trilogy: the 1895 war reaches its conclusion as Imani and Germano's fates converge in the ruins of the Gaza Empire.

en: Jesusalem (Biblioasis, 2012, tr. David Brookshaw)
bl: A father keeps his sons isolated in the wilderness — when a woman arrives everything unravels. Richly symbolic.
Newspaper chronicles meditating on language, identity and everyday Mozambican life.
Early journalistic chronicles that established Mia Couto's reputation as a prose stylist and social observer.
Essays on Africa, identity and global politics following Obama's election — characteristically playful and sharp.
Collection of Couto's celebrated newspaper chronicles on love, language and African life.
Recent Mia Couto stories continuing his lyrical exploration of Mozambican realities.

en: Niketche: A Story of Polygamy (Ayebia Clarke, 2021, tr. David Brookshaw)
aw: Prémio José Craveirinha de Literatura 2003; Camões Prize 2021 (career)
bl: A police officer's wife discovers his multiple relationships and decides to meet the other women — bold novel on polygamy and female autonomy.
Two communities — one fleeing soldiers, one fleeing drought — converge in catastrophe. Epic, biblical in scope.
First novel by a Mozambican woman: navigating love, marriage and freedom between tradition and modernity.
A mulatta woman searches for her roots across Mozambican history from slavery to independence.
Seminal anti-colonial poems voicing Black identity and Pan-African solidarity. Circulated in mimeograph for 50 years before formal publication.

en: We Killed Mangy-Dog (Heinemann, 1969, tr. Dorothy Guedes)
bl: Written when Honwana was nineteen and under house arrest — stories of children in colonial Mozambique. Quietly devastating.
Stories of urban Mozambican life, particularly women navigating domestic violence and poverty. Precise and politically alert.
Two men on opposite banks of the Zambezi watch a woman who connects them — about longing, land and the river as historical actor.
Set in colonial Beira, reconstructing the layered social world of a coastal city through meticulous historical detail.
Ten stories exposing Mozambican patriarchal traditions. The title story: a woman forced to bear a child with her brother-in-law to produce a male heir.

t: O Osso Côncavo e Outros Poemas
aw: Oceanos shortlist 2018; Prémio Nacional de Poesia Moçambique 1995
bl: Considered 'probably the greatest living Mozambican poet' — interweaves memory, jazz rhythms and atmospheric Maputo.
Later Patraquim collection — 'Pemba for chronic arsonists' — poetry of provocation and combustion.
A Mozambican lawyer in a provincial town navigates the complex legacies of independence and traditional authority.
Short fiction by one of Mozambique's most prolific story-writers, blending tradition and modernity.
Novel exploring the tensions of urban Mozambican neighbourhood life.

t: O Último Olhar de Manú Miranda
bl: Set in Portuguese Goa's final decades — explores memory and ancestral identity. Father of former European Council President António Costa.
Personal narrative of life across decades of political change in Mozambique.
Mozambican poetry series exploring grief and the weight of mortality.

t: O Testamento do Sr. Napumoceno da Silva Araújo
en: The Last Will and Testament of Senhor da Silva Araújo (Heinemann, 1991)
bl: A Cape Verdean merchant's scandalous will reveals a secret life. A Dickensian comic masterpiece of São Vicente social life.
Gentle, warm novel about an amateur poet on São Vicente and the community that forms around his work.
Two brothers — one successful, one dissolute — reflect on diverging lives. A study in Cape Verdean masculinity.
Stories blending realism and the marvellous set on the Cape Verde archipelago.
A Cape Verdean travels to Goa and encounters the last traces of Portuguese colonial culture in India.
Picaresque comic novel — a dead man who refuses to stay dead causes social chaos across the islands.
Novel exploring the island's complex relationship with tropical identity and colonial legacy.
Theatrical texts and domestic scenes from Germano Almeida's playful Cape Verdean world.
The foundational Cape Verdean novel: a boy's coming-of-age on São Nicolau island, shadowed by drought and emigration.
A community devastated by the easterly wind that kills crops and provokes famine — stark naturalist novel of survival.

aw: Camões Prize 2009 — first Cape Verdean laureate
bl: Poetic notebooks exploring literary myth and philosophical disenchantment — allusive, cosmopolitan, unusual in Cape Verdean letters.
Classic Cape Verdean novella capturing rhythms of Creole island life in Santo Antão with poetic realism. Author died at 96 in 2020.
Cape Verdean poetry collection exploring the boundaries between the natural and the constructed.
Second Haideia Avelino Pires collection: connections between naming and being in Cape Verdean verse.
A novel from São Tomé e Príncipe exploring island life, colonial memory and female experience.

a: Aniceto Afonso & Carlos de Matos Gomes
bl: Comprehensive history of Portugal's colonial wars (1961–74) by two veteran officers — the definitive reference on Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau.
Study of Gungunhana, last Gaza king, and his resistance to Portuguese colonialism.
Series on Kongo cultural heritage and oral traditions.

t: Dona Flor e Seus Dois Maridos
en: Dona Flor and Her Two Husbands (Knopf, 1969, tr. Harriet de Onís)
bl: A Bahian cooking teacher haunted by her dissolute first husband's ghost after remarrying — exuberant, sensual comedy of desire, food and magic.

en: Captains of the Sands (Penguin Classics, 2013, tr. Gregory Rabassa)
aw: Camões Prize 1995 (career); 808 copies burned by Vargas, 1937
bl: A gang of street children on Salvador's docks — his all-time bestseller at 4.3 million copies and a foundational Afro-Brazilian novel.

en: Jubiabá (Avon, 1984, tr. Margaret A. Neves)
bl: A young Black man from Bahia's slums becomes a boxer and political activist — steeped in Candomblé, capoeira and Afro-Brazilian resistance.

en: The Violent Land (Knopf, 1945, tr. Samuel Putnam)
bl: Two families fight for land in the Bahian cacao zone — Amado's grimmest novel: a saga of violence, greed and forest clearing.

en: The Golden Harvest (Avon, 1992)
bl: Sequel to Terras do Sem-Fim: the decline of the Bahian cacao barons as foreign capital takes over the trade.

en: The War of the Saints (Bantam, 1993, tr. Gregory Rabassa)
bl: The Virgin Mary's statue joins the Candomblé orishas — late Amado celebrating Bahian religious syncretism.

en: Shepherds of the Night (Knopf, 1967, tr. Harriet de Onís)
bl: Bahian bohemians, prostitutes and capoeira fighters under the protection of the Candomblé deity Ogum.

t: A Morte e a Morte de Quincas Berro Dágua
en: The Two Deaths of Quincas Wateryell (Avon, 1965)
bl: A dead Bahian man apparently gets up from his wake and returns to his bohemian life — a delirious carnivalesque fable.
Social realist portrait of a crowded tenement in Salvador, Bahia — Amado's proletarian third novel.

en: Home is the Sailor (Knopf, 1964)
bl: Two novellas set in Bahia's port town Ilhéus: the captain who reinvents himself and the miraculous saint.
Brutal lives of labourers on cacao plantations. The first edition was seized by police as 'socialist literature'.

en: Turbulence (Bloomsbury, 1992, tr. Peter Bush)
bl: An unnamed narrator drifts through a Kafkaesque Rio, pursued by vague threats — Brazil's most celebrated songwriter's startling novelistic debut.

en: Benjamin (Grove Press, 1997, tr. Clifford E. Landers)
bl: A former model becomes obsessed with a young woman who resembles his dead lover from the years of military dictatorship.

es.pub: Fondo Editorial Casa de las Américas

en: Budapest (Grove Press, 2004, tr. Alison Entrekin)
bl: A ghostwriter travels to Budapest and becomes entangled in a double life across two languages and two cities.

A memoir-novel of Buarque's childhood in Rome in 1953–54: bicycle routes mapped on a bedroom wall, first desires, letters to a schoolgirl called Sandy L., and Vargas's suicide heard from afar. Published when he was 80.

en: Spilt Milk (Grove Press, 2012, tr. Clifford Landers)
bl: A centenarian patriarch dictates his memoirs to an unseen listener, his narrative dissolving into unreliable memory and racial fantasy — Buarque's most formally ambitious novel.

en: My German Brother (Grove Press, 2017, tr. Flora Thomson-DeVeaux)
bl: A young man in 1970s Rio discovers evidence of a half-brother in Nazi Germany — based loosely on Buarque's own family history.

en: Lead Years (Grove Press, 2024, tr. Flora Thomson-DeVeaux)
bl: An ageing man pieces together fragmentary memories of the years of Brazilian military dictatorship.

en: The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas (Oxford, 2020, tr. Flora Thomson-DeVeaux)
bl: A deceased man narrates his life with mordant cynicism from beyond the grave — the founding text of Brazilian realism, startlingly modern.

en: Dom Casmurro (Oxford, 1997, tr. John Gledson)
bl: An aging man reconstructs his marriage to Capitu — one of literature's most debated characters. Did she betray him?

en: The Alienist (Melville House, 2013, tr. William L. Grossman) / The Psychiatrist (UC Press, 1963)
bl: Dr Simão Bacamarte returns to the small town of Itaguaí, establishes an asylum, and progressively expands his definition of madness until most of the town is locked up — then turns the logic on itself. A devastating satire of scientific rationalism and the arbitrary nature of normality. Often cited as one of the finest novellas in any language.

en: The Passion According to G.H. (New Directions, 1988, tr. Ronald W. Sousa)
bl: A society woman kills a cockroach and is plunged into metaphysical crisis — relentless ecstatic monologue about disgust and transcendence. Her masterpiece.

en: The Hour of the Star (Carcanet, 1986, tr. Giovanni Pontiero)
bl: A male narrator tells the story of Macabéa, a migrant girl in Rio — Lispector's final novel: meditation on narration, poverty and the ethics of fiction.
Collected newspaper chronicles — intimate, strange, funny and wise. A domestic, self-deprecating, infinitely curious Lispector.
Complete letters of Clarice Lispector, revealing a more vulnerable and professionally complex woman than the hermetic novelist of legend.

en: Barren Lives (University of Texas Press, 1965, tr. Ralph Edward Dimmick)
bl: A family of nordestinos and their dog migrate across the parched sertão — fragmentary episodes including one narrated from the dog's point of view.

en: Prison Memoirs (Soho Press, 2019, tr. Thomas Colchie)
bl: Ramos's account of his imprisonment by Vargas's regime 1936–37 — honest, unflinching and devoid of heroism.

en: São Bernardo (Calderbooks, 1975)
bl: A brutal landowner narrates his life and the destruction of his marriage — a study in unreliable narration and patriarchal violence.
Ramos's debut: a small-town clerk attempts to write a novel about the Caeté Indians while entangled in adultery.

en: The Devil to Pay in the Backlands (Knopf, 1963, tr. James L. Taylor & Harriet de Onís)
bl: A retired bandit delivers an unbroken monologue — a linguistic tornado in which Rosa invents language itself. Among the greatest 20th-century novels.

en: Time and the Wind (Macmillan, 1951 — first volume only)
bl: Trilogy spanning 200 years of Rio Grande do Sul history — monumental Brazilian historical fiction, beloved in the south.

t: As Mentiras que os Homens Contam
bl: Brazil's most popular humorist on the everyday lies men tell — to mothers, wives and friends. Ironic brevity and warmth.

en: Crooked Plow (Verso, 2023, tr. Johnny Lorenz)
aw: Jabuti Prize 2020; Oceanos Prize 2020; LeYa Prize 2018; International Booker shortlist 2024
bl: Two sisters on a quilombo-descended settlement carry a trauma whose source is gradually revealed — land, Afro-Brazilian religion and slavery's afterlives.
A couple on a remote farm confront forces — human and supernatural — that threaten everything they have built.
Lyrical third novel continuing Vieira Junior's exploration of Afro-Brazilian rural life and resistance.
A woman's odyssey through the Brazilian interior — ironic reimagining of classical epic rooted in Black Brazilian experience.

en: Child of the Dark (E.P. Dutton, 1962, tr. David St. Clair) / Beyond All Pity (UK)
aw: 1 million+ copies; translated into 40+ countries; foundational Afro-Brazilian literature
bl: Diary by a Black single mother in São Paulo's Canindé favela. 10,000 copies sold in the first week — Brazil's biggest-ever bestseller at the time.

aw: Casa de las Américas Prize; Jabuti finalist
bl: Epic 950-page historical novel narrated by Kehinde, an enslaved woman separated from her son — meticulously reconstructed Afro-Brazilian life across two continents.

t: Memórias de um Sargento de Milícias
en: Memoirs of a Militia Sergeant (Oxford, 1999, tr. Ronald W. Sousa)
bl: Foundational picaresque set in Johannine Rio de Janeiro following the lovable rogue Leonardo — origin of the 'malandro' archetype.

en: The Slum (Oxford, 2000, tr. David H. Rosenthal)
bl: The pinnacle of Brazilian naturalism: a Rio tenement as an organic, growing entity — searing portrait of race, class and greed.
Azevedo's earlier naturalist novel: a boarding house in Rio as arena for social transgression and moral decay.

en: Ancient Tillage (Penguin Classics, 2016, tr. Karen Sherwood Sotelino)
bl: Through the parable of the Prodigal Son: a young man from a Lebanese immigrant farming family consumed by desire and rebellion against his patriarch.

en: The Vampire of Curitiba (Knopf, 1972, tr. Gregory Rabassa)
bl: Nelsinho, a sex-obsessed predator, prowls Curitiba — inverted moral fables in razor-sharp prose. Trevisan died December 2024, aged 99.
Masterpiece of the Sugarcane Cycle: three protagonists embodying the collapse of Northeast Brazil's feudal plantation society after abolition.

en: Plantation Boy (Knopf, 1966, tr. Emmi Baum — omnibus)
bl: First of the Sugarcane Cycle: a boy sent to his grandfather's plantation after witnessing his mother's violent death.
Part of the 'cangaço cycle': messianic religious movements and banditry in the Brazilian sertão, drawn from real historical incidents.

en: Quarup (Knopf, 1970, tr. Barbara Shelby)
bl: An idealistic priest dreams of a Jesuit utopia among the indigenous Xingu — the 1964 military coup shatters everything.

en: I'm Still Here (forthcoming in English)
aw: Jabuti Prize 2015; film: Oscar Best International Feature 2025
bl: His mother Eunice Paiva reinvented herself as a human rights lawyer after her husband was disappeared by the dictatorship in 1971. Adapted by Walter Salles.

en: The Sun on My Head (FSG / Faber, 2019, tr. Julia Sanches)
aw: FT Book of the Year; Edinburgh First Book Award longlist
bl: Boys and young men growing up in Rio's favelas. First Brazilian to sell translation rights to nine countries before a debut's release.

en: Blood-Drenched Beard (Hamish Hamilton, 2014, tr. Alison Entrekin)
bl: A face-blind young man moves to a coastal town to investigate his grandfather's unsolved murder — masterful existential noir.

en: There Were Many Horses (Amazon Crossing, 2014)
aw: APCA Award; Machado de Assis Award
bl: One day in São Paulo as 69 fragments in wildly different registers — revolutionised contemporary Brazilian fiction.

en: The House in Smyrna (Scribe, 2015, tr. Alison Entrekin)
bl: A woman takes her grandfather's house key to Smyrna — weaves displacement across Turkey, Brazil and Portugal through three generations.
Levy's most recent novel — continuing her exploration of trauma, migration and the stories we keep from ourselves.

en: Bury Your Dead (Charco Press, forthcoming 2026)
bl: Edgar Wilson collects road-kill animals; when he finds a woman's corpse and police lack resources, he and a priest give the dead dignity. Brutalist prose.

en: His Own Man (Other Press, 2014, tr. Kim M. Hastings)
bl: A diplomat makes a Faustian pact with Brazil's military regime, becoming involved in Operation Condor activities in Uruguay and Chile.
Two timelines: a magnate's 1970s party; present-day Ouro Preto where 'God is dead' graffiti connects to the decades-old mystery. By the Titãs guitarist.
A woman narrates a hundred years of family life in formally inventive verse-like prose — a debut of great emotional force.
Epic family saga based on five years of research into the author's own ancestry, spanning the 19th-century slave trade to the 20th century.

en: The Secret Dinner (Celadon Books, forthcoming 2026)
bl: Montes's most critically praised work — exploring cannibalism and obsession with dark wit.
A daring fictional diary imagining what Graciliano Ramos might have written on his release from prison in 1937 — hybrid of biography, fiction and essay.
A retired professor traces his lifelong friendship with a journalist consumed by drugs and rock'n'roll — meditation on love, loss and homosexuality.

en: Moldy Strawberries (Restless Books, 2022, tr. Bruna Dantas Lobato)
bl: Complete stories: intensely lyrical, queer, consumed by longing and the dark textures of urban life in the dictatorship and AIDS years.

en: The Eternal Son (Tagus Press, 2012, tr. Alison Entrekin)
aw: Jabuti Prize 2008; Prémio São Paulo de Literatura 2008
bl: A father narrates the first years of his son's life after a Down syndrome diagnosis — brutally honest about initial rejection.

en: Bay of All Saints (Viking, 1992, tr. Giovanni Pontiero)
bl: 17th-century Salvador: the power struggle between a corrupt governor and Father António Vieira's faction. Credited with renewing the Brazilian historical novel.

en: High Art (Harper & Row, 1986, tr. Ellen Watson)
bl: A lawyer-turned-detective investigates murders where victims are found with a letter carved into their skin. Brazil's landmark crime novel.

en: Macunaíma (Random House, 1984, tr. E.A. Goodland)
bl: A shapeshifting hero without character travels through Brazilian mythology and modernity — the ur-text of Brazilian Modernism.

en: An Invincible Memory (Harper & Row, 1989, tr. João Ubaldo Ribeiro)
bl: Four centuries of Brazilian history seen from below — through slaves, soldiers, tricksters and saints. A carnivalesque masterpiece.
A man spends a single day scraping together money to pay his milkman — relentless naturalist novel of economic pressure.
Three cousins traverse the Inhamuns sertão to visit their dying patriarch — reinvents the literary sertão beyond Guimarães Rosa.

en: The Land (Readers International, 1987)
bl: Nelo leaves the Bahian sertão for São Paulo only to return broken and suicidal — 150,000+ copies; translated into 18+ languages.
A dystopian fable — people walk in circles under tyranny — allegorising both Salazar's Portugal and Brazil's dictatorship.

en: The End (Restless Books)
aw: Jabuti Prize for Brazilian Book Published Abroad
bl: Torres's debut novel on mortality and memory — sold 200,000+ copies. By Brazil's Cannes Best Actress and 2025 Oscar-nominated actress.
Collections of Fernanda Torres's sharp, funny chronicles on Brazilian culture and politics.

en: Ponciá Vicêncio (Host Publications, 2007, tr. Paloma Costa)
bl: A Black woman moves from a rural fazenda to an urban favela — Evaristo's pioneering novel of Afro-Brazilian women's experience.
A favela community is demolished and its inhabitants scattered — Evaristo's lyrical, collective portrait of displacement.

en: Diary of the Fall (Harvill Secker, 2014, tr. Margaret Jull Costa)
aw: Jabuti Prize; São Paulo Prize for Literature
bl: Three generations of Jewish-Brazilian men haunted by the Holocaust and by a teenage fall at a bar mitzvah — a profound meditation on inherited trauma.

en: Brown and Yellow (Restless Books, 2023, tr. Daniel Hahn)
bl: Twin brothers — one who passes as white, one who identifies as Black — navigate racial identity in contemporary Brazil.

t: É Sempre a Hora da Nossa Morte Amém
bl: Debut novel tracing four generations of a Brazilian family across violence, faith and survival.
Debut novel set in the Brazilian sertão exploring drought, violence and the sacred.
Stories of women navigating violence, desire and social constraint — from Brazil's Angolan-heritage prize-winning author.
The 1915 Great Drought in Ceará told through two cousins — the foundational northeastern Brazilian novel, by the first woman elected to the Brazilian Academy of Letters.

aw: Two Jabuti Prizes for a debut — unprecedented
bl: An instant classic of Brazilian urban literature: pool hall sharks, hustlers and vagrants in brilliantly stylised popular oral language.
The major collection by Brazil's most celebrated confessional poet, who died at 31 — erotic, fragmentary, formally radical.
Contemporary Brazilian novel — visible on shelf among recent Brazilian fiction.
Novel by Bernardo Carvalho, one of Brazil's most formally inventive contemporary writers.
Brazilian short fiction anthology collecting contemporary voices across regions and generations.

en: Multitudinous Heart (FSG, 2015, tr. Richard Zenith) — selection
bl: Complete poems of Brazil's greatest modern poet: ironic, melancholy, tender — from 'Poema de Sete Faces' to late meditations on time and death.

en: The Mystical Rose (Bloodaxe, 2014, tr. Ellen Doré Watson)
bl: The comprehensive two-volume Global Editora edition of Cecília Meireles's complete poems — the standard scholarly text.
First of the complete poetry volumes: metaphysical, musical and melancholy, drawing on sea, time and mortality with extraordinary formal mastery.

en: The Mystical Rose / The Alphabet in the Park (Bloodaxe / Wesleyan UP, tr. Ellen Doré Watson)
bl: Debut collection championed by Drummond: Catholic mysticism fused with sensual domestic life in provincial Minas Gerais. Published at 40.

en: Birds for a Demolition (Carnegie Mellon UP, 2010, tr. Idra Novey)
bl: Poetry made from insects, 'useless utensils' and small aquatic creatures — a child's astonished gaze at the Pantanal. Drummond called Barros 'Brazil's greatest poet'.
Dramatic poem about the execution of Frei Caneca, hero of the 1824 Confederation of the Equator — Brazil's most austere modernist poet at his most political.

en: Tropical Truth (Knopf / Bloomsbury, 2002, tr. Isabel de Sena)
bl: Intellectual memoir: Bahian childhood, genesis of Tropicália, imprisonment and exile in London during the dictatorship, and reflections on Brazilian identity.
The definitive three-volume biography of Getúlio Vargas — Brazil's most important 20th-century political figure: populist, authoritarian, tragic.
Rich reconstruction of Rio de Janeiro in the 1920s — journalism, music, architecture, football and nightlife by Brazil's foremost biographer.
Ruy Castro's biography of playwright and provocateur Nelson Rodrigues — brilliant, outrageous and compulsively readable.
Study of Patrícia Rehder Galvão (Pagu) — Modernist artist, writer, Communist militant and Brazil's first female political prisoner.
A Brazilian-Japanese family saga spanning decades of immigration and cultural negotiation in Paraná state.

t: O Ouvidor do Brasil: 99 Vezes Tom Jobim
bl: Ruy Castro's portrait of Tom Jobim through 99 vignettes and encounters — Brazil's definitive Jobim book.
Biography of the iconoclast Brazilian singer and Secos e Molhados frontman — pioneer of androgynous rock in 1970s Brazil.
Portrait of the Tropicália co-founder, former Minister of Culture and global icon of Brazilian MPB and axé music.
Overview of Brazilian popular music from samba to MPB — histories, song analysis and cultural context.
Comprehensive reference dictionary covering composers, performers, styles and vocabulary of Brazilian samba.
Portrait of João Gilberto, bossa nova's founding genius and Brazil's most elusive musical figure.
Lira Neto's writings on Brazilian culture and music, alongside his Getúlio Vargas biography.

en: A Concise History of Brazil (Cambridge UP, 1999, tr. Arthur Brakel)
bl: The standard one-volume history of Brazil from pre-colonial times to the present — accessible and authoritative.
Definitive modern biography of Joaquim José da Silva Xavier (Tiradentes), hero of the 1789 Inconfidência Mineira — Brazil's foundational independence martyr.

t: Escravidão Indígena nos Sertões de Piratauba
bl: Academic study of indigenous enslavement in the colonial Brazilian sertão — essential for understanding colonial labour systems.
Accessible introduction to Candomblé — its orishas, rituals, history and relationship to Afro-Brazilian identity.
Classic work of Brazilian folklore scholarship mapping the distribution of myths and legends across the country's regions. The founding father of Brazilian folklorology.
Study of Abdias Nascimento — playwright, founder of the Black Experimental Theatre, senator and tireless advocate for Afro-Brazilian rights.
Multi-volume series on political repression and resistance during Brazil's military dictatorship (1964–85).
Academic series on religious diversity in Brazil — Candomblé, Spiritism, Evangelical Christianity and Catholicism.
Study of Black Brazil — demographics, culture, politics and the ongoing struggle for racial equality.
Multi-volume academic history of Brazil covering political, social and cultural development across major periods.

t: O Mito do Golpe do Brasil
bl: Critical examination of the mythology surrounding Brazil's various coups — 1930, 1945, 1964 — and their lasting legacies.
